properties.digitized_from: DataSF Assessor parcels (acdm-wktn), lot 4110013 (recorded 2019-02-07; mapped 2019-03-14; active); cross-checked against Pier 70 Design for Development Figure 6.4.2 - Building Height Maximum (p.155).
properties.digitization_method: REDONE 2026-09-14: the previous version of this polygon was traced using a transform fit from 5 street intersections plus Historic Building 12's real footprint as a 6th anchor. A user-flagged visual comparison against satellite imagery showed the resulting blocks were systematically rotated/sheared (~13-14 degrees off, and not even mutually orthogonal) relative to the real street grid -- confirmed by comparing traced block bearings against the real, independently-surveyed Building 14 footprint (DataSF Building Footprints, blklot 4052001), which sits at the real street grid's true orientation (~356/86 degrees, consistent with SF's known ~4-degree grid skew). Root cause: an error in the original corner-correspondence matching, not a diagram-scan distortion. REBUILT using a fresh 6-point affine transform: 5 real street-intersection control points (20th St x Illinois St, 20th St x Michigan St, 21st St x Illinois St, 21st St x Michigan St, 22nd St x Illinois St -- fetched from OpenStreetMap via this project's own src/fetch_streets.py) plus the real, independently-confirmed centroid of Historic Building 12's own Assessor parcel (blklot 4114010) as a 6th, spatially-distant anchor. This fit has a residual error of 1-8m against its own 6 control points (far tighter than the previous transform), AND was validated by checking that it reproduces the correct real-world bearing (independently confirmed via Building 14's footprint) rather than just checking point-position error, which is what let the previous version's shear go undetected. Pixel corners for this block were re-read directly from Figure 6.4.2 with fresh, fine-grained crops. Residual error against the 6 control points is roughly 1-8m; treat vertex positions as accurate to roughly 5-15m given the additional (small) error from reading this specific block's own corners off the diagram. CORRECTED 2026-09-14 (second pass, same day): after the shear fix above, a user-flagged visual check still showed this block overlapping paved streets. Root cause found: several blocks (PKN, PKS, HDY3, HDY1/2, E4) had their OWN corner pixel positions misread during transcription -- e.g. PKN's west edge was recorded as pixel x=163 when the diagram's own gridline labels put it at x=355 (which is where the Illinois St anchor point itself was measured). This was a transcription slip, not a transform error -- the 6-point transform's anchors were unaffected (confirmed: A, B, C1, C2, D, E1, E2, E3, F/G, H1, H2 were read correctly the first time). Re-read all 5 affected blocks' corners directly against their crop images' own labeled gridlines and recomputed. CORRECTED 2026-09-14 (sixth pass): user-flagged check found a real gap between PKN's south edge and PKS's own north edge -- both blocks were transformed/traced independently and didn't agree on where their shared internal boundary sits, leaving an ~8-11m strip of real, currently-parked-in pavement claimed by neither polygon. User pointed out the real match is not the warehouse building across the street, but the large vacant/graded lot on the WEST side of Illinois St, between roughly 20th and 21st St -- its silhouette (elongated, tilted a few degrees off true north, matching the local curb bearing) is the same shape being traced, just larger. Re-traced directly from that lot's own visible boundary: anchored on two points read off the lot's real east edge (the Illinois St curb, high-contrast and unambiguous), which gave a measured bearing of ~182.3/272.3 degrees. CORRECTED same day: user caught that this made the east edge visibly non-parallel to the real curb -- the two curb points used for that bearing were only ~13m apart (an 80m along-curb baseline but just ~3.5m of east-west offset between them), so a 1-2 pixel misreading at zoom 20 (~0.3-0.6m each) was enough to swing the derived bearing by several degrees -- exactly the 'reading points too close together, small errors don't cancel' failure this project's bearing_trace.py already warns about, repeated instead of heeded. Fixed by using this site's already-established, multiply-validated grid bearing (176.5/356.5 degrees, from Historic Building 14's real surveyed footprint, and consistent with Block B's own independently-confirmed ~175 degrees) instead of re-deriving a fresh one from a short noisy baseline; kept the same real anchor point and the same independently-measured distances (~126m north-south, ~51m east-west). SECOND CORRECTION, same day: user caught that the resulting rectangle still overlapped the street -- the anchor point itself (read near a crosswalk with parked cars and shadow clutter) was actually ~8-9m INSIDE the road, not on the curb, even though the bearing was by then correct. Root cause: misread the sidewalk/asphalt color transition in a cluttered spot. Re-read the curb at two clean, unobstructed points well clear of any crosswalk (via a brightness-transition scan of the sidewalk-to-asphalt boundary at zoom 20, cross-checked against the pixel-to-lonlat math directly rather than by eye), which independently reproduced the same 176.57 degree bearing (confirming the established bearing was never the problem) but placed the curb about 8.5m further west than the previous anchor. Extrapolated the corrected curb line to the same north/south extents and rebuilt the west edge at the same 51m width. Overlay-checked both the north and south corners individually afterward: the east edge now sat on the sidewalk side of the curb along its whole length, not on the asphalt. THIRD CORRECTION, same day: user pointed out the east edge was still at the OUTER (curb) side of the public Illinois St sidewalk, meaning the polygon's area included the whole ~4.5m-wide public sidewalk itself, not just the private lot -- and that the south edge (the cross-street's own sidewalk/crosswalk) had the identical problem, cutting straight through the crosswalk stripe pattern rather than stopping at the back of that sidewalk. Fixed both: re-read the INNER (lot-side/back-of-sidewalk) edge of the Illinois St sidewalk, at the dirt-to-concrete color transition on the lot side rather than the concrete-to-asphalt transition on the street side (found ~4.5m west of the previous curb-line anchor, at the same validated 176.5 degree bearing -- confirms this project's east edges up to now, including PKN/PKS/E1/E2/HDY3 etc., were anchored on curbs; worth re-checking whether any of those also failed to exclude a real sidewalk). Re-read the south edge similarly: found the true back-of-sidewalk transition on the lot side of the cross-street's own sidewalk (north of its crosswalk stripes, not through them) and rebuilt the south edge through that point, perpendicular to the same established bearing, solving for new SE/SW corners as the intersection with the (unchanged) east and west edge lines. Overlay-confirmed the south edge now runs clear of the crosswalk stripes along its whole length. FOURTH CORRECTION (negligible, ~0.17m): when generalizing this fix into a reusable, tested function (bearing_trace.rectangle_from_four_edges, added along with src/test_bearing_trace.py), recomputing NE from the same raw measured anchors gave a corner ~0.17m from the hand-computed one above (accumulated rounding across several manual correction passes) -- adjusted NE to match the function's output exactly, so the file and the tested reconstruction agree bit-for-bit rather than by coincidence. See src/test_bearing_trace.py for the from-scratch reconstruction this geometry must continue to match. properties.regulatory_context: Bethlehem Steel HQ, a 1917 neoclassical office building designed by Frederick H. Meyer. Its size is reported differently: RH's May 13, 2022 release calls it an '80,000-Square-Foot Landmark Building', the National Register nomination says it 'contains 56,268 square feet', and the Port gives 61,311 sq ft before and 60,525 sq ft after rehabilitation (HPC packet, Nov 2013; Port Item 12A, Jan 2019); no source settles the difference. Its floors are described differently too: the HPC packet says 'a five-story above street level office building' with 'two lower levels and a penthouse level', the nomination describes three full stories over a basement and sub-basement with a partial fourth floor and penthouse, and RH says 'five floors'. Rehabbed by Orton Development Inc. (ODI) starting after a Nov 26 2013 Historic Preservation Commission review (sfplanning.org HPC packet 2013.1168E); per that packet, the seismic upgrade uses shear walls, and the rehab preserves the historic exterior elevations while adapting the interior. The Port's Jan 2019 update reported Buildings 101 and 102 still under construction, with completion and occupancy of Building 101 anticipated in 2020. RH announced the opening of RH San Francisco -- 'The Gallery at the Historic Bethlehem Steel Building' (showroom, Palm Court restaurant and two wine bars, rooftop park) in a press release dated May 13, 2022; the release gives no separate opening day, and no independent dated report was read.

This is a case where the diagram's own simplified box undersold the real building's true extent -- the real, surveyed footprint takes priority, consistent with how this project treats real building data everywhere else. properties.regulatory_context: Union Iron Works Machine Shop and Foundry, Buildings 113/114, on the south side of 20th Street just east of Illinois Street -- 'one of the most valuable and most vulnerable historic resources on the site' per the 2013 HPC packet (2013.1168E). Two unreinforced brick structures (built in 1885 and 1886 per one passage of the HPC packet, while its rehabilitation plans and Port Item 12A, Jan 2019, say 'built from 1885-1888'; the National Register nomination says the eastern, 1885 portion housed the blacksmith and boiler shop and the western, 1886 portion the machine shop) joined in 1914 by a reinforced concrete connector; building-length skylights, rows of high arched windows; ~95,000 GSF, 492ft long by 175ft wide, ~62ft tall. Buildings 115 and 116 abut Building 113/114, constructed 1916-1917, ~38,000 GSF, 57ft tall, with 'unusual windows and monitor skylights.' At review time the complex was red-tagged and subject to an engineer's advisory of imminent collapse. Rehab by Orton Development Inc. (ODI) was proposed (HPC packet) to include 'abatement, demolition or relocation of metal additions to the building on the western and southern facades', a new steel seismic system tied into the brick perimeter, and demolition of two minor eastern appendages (Buildings 23/24, ~1,500 GSF). Proposed for industrial/warehouse/maker-space use (food, tech, life science, biotech, education, arts production) with ancillary office, showroom, and retail, alongside Building 14, framing a shared ~45,000 sf courtyard.

Georeferenced using 9 real street-intersection control points fetched from OpenStreetMap via this project's own src/fetch_streets.py, fit as a least-squares affine transform. NOTE: an initial attempt also used the real, confirmed positions of the Sophie Maxwell Building and the UCSF Block 2 building as anchors, but they produced 50-60m of error against the street-only fit -- this diagram is dated Feb 26, 2020, predating UCSF's ~2023-24 arrival as a life-science anchor tenant, so those two real buildings likely do not sit where this 2020 figure's own numbered blocks would place them (their own real parcels are used directly elsewhere in this dataset and were NOT re-derived from this diagram). The final transform here uses street intersections only. Residual error against those control points is roughly 8-24m. Traced polygons were additionally clipped against the real, confirmed Sophie Maxwell and UCSF Block 2 parcels (and against Prequel Park's approximate geometry) so this speculative tracing never overrides real or better-sourced geometry. Re-traced this block's own corner pixels the same way and ran them through the new transform. This corrected transform disagrees with the original 9-point affine transform by tens of meters in places -- e.g. it revealed the original trace had Blocks 3/4 shifted east into the excavation pit/street area, and Blocks 11/12 roughly 2x too deep -- and the new positions now land within real, distinct site features (buildings, graded lots) visible in satellite imagery rather than straddling roads. Known residual limitation: GCP street positions are centerline-based (matching OSM convention), while a block boundary should sit at the near curb, so any edge close to a GCP street can land a few meters into that street after transformation -- checked for and corrected on this block's street-facing edge(s) where applicable using this project's already-established grid bearing (356.5 deg) and, where available, an independently diagram-measured depth/width. properties.regulatory_context: Station A: the site's historic 1901 unreinforced-brick turbine hall (a four-story brick structure per the 2018 Draft EIR), vacant/unoccupied. The design review approves adaptive reuse into approximately 403,750 GSF of office (the Planning Commission granted the office allocation on Oct 22, 2020, Motion 20801) via an eight-story vertical addition above the retained historic shell and a public mid-block passage through the building (the design-review memo describes it as accessible from both Georgia Lane and Power Station Park in one place, and as connecting Georgia Lane and Louisiana Paseo in another), designed by Herzog & de Meuron with Adamson Associates; the Planning Director approved the Design Review Application on March 2, 2022. The design-review memo gives a total height of 205 feet measured from grade for the Station A building with its eight-story addition, but also says the addition is 'subject to the prevailing 145-foot and 160-foot building height maximums', and the D4D's Figure 6.2.3 labels the block's two strips 145' and 160'; the sources read do not reconcile the two figures. The Chronicle (July 29, 2026) reports a requested Development Agreement amendment that would let Station A grow by 30 feet; it is not shown here as enacted. Construction of the addition had not started per SF YIMBY (Aug 27, 2025) and the 2024 annual compliance report (March 2025), which describes only 2024 brick stabilization work. The 2018 Draft EIR project proposed demolishing Station A (its Alternative D retained it); SF YIMBY (June 2021) says the adaptive reuse was included following community pushback against demolition, and no source found names who advocated for it.

The median's physical description rests on this repository's own trace. 2026-10-02: public-text pass. accuracy_caveat, digitized_from reworded for readers (meaning unchanged; no change to the shape, status, use or geometry_type); previous wording -- accuracy_caveat: 'APPROXIMATE -- owner-guided satellite trace, idealized to a fitted semicircle rather than left as a raw hand-traced outline. The repo's copy of DataSF's Parcels - Active and Retired dataset (data_as_of 2026-05-31) carries three active secured-roll parcels lying wholly inside it (8701004, 700 4th St; 8701003, 311 Townsend St; 8700001, 797 7th St; together about 82% of its area), so the earlier statement that the rail right-of-way carries no block/lot was wrong. Three of the four sides (Townsend, 4th, 7th) are real, continuous DataSF street centerlines; the fourth (King St plus a straight closing line at the I-280 interchange, drawn on the earlier belief that King's DataSF centerline ended short of 7th; see the correction in digitized_from) is the weakest edge and the one most likely to need revision if a real project boundary or EIR figure becomes available. Includes the existing Caltrain 4th & King Street Station itself, which the project's own description treats as part of the site being redeveloped, not something outside it.'; digitized_from: 'Bounded by DataSF's official street centerlines (data/raw/official_street_centerlines.geojson): Townsend St (4th-7th) on the north, 4th St (Townsend-King) on the east, 7th St (Townsend-King) on the west, and King St (4th-~6th) on the south, each buffered by the project's standard measured half-width (src/street_geometry.py, 6.8m) and inset from the outer street-to-street ring by that same half-width to approximate the curb/yard edge rather than the street centerline itself -- same method as P9 (data/manual/mission_bay_p9_open_space.geojson). 2026-09-29 audit correction: the earlier text here said King St's DataSF centerline stops short of 7th St. It does not: the file has King St segments from 6th to 7th St (06TH ST -> 07TH ST, (-122.398585, 37.77289) to (-122.400804, 37.771138), plus '06TH ST - END: WEST' and 'END: EAST - 07TH ST' pieces); only the 5th-6th St segment ends at (-122.397986, 37.773324), and the next segment begins about 70 m further on. I-280 ramp segments are in the file too. The resulting inset polygon is 20.08 acres, matching the SF Planning/Caltrain FAQ's own '20-acre site' description almost exactly, and its outline was checked directly against Esri World Imagery (via contextily) overlaid in QGIS-equivalent fashion -- it tracks the real fan of tracks and the 4th & King station platform canopy tightly, confirmed by the site owner 2026-09-21 after a side-by-side review of the overlay.'; notes: 'SF Planning Case No. 2023-000384CWP, 'SF Railyards Planning Program'. The 20-acre site at the nexus of SoMa, Mission Bay and Showplace Square: Caltrain's northern terminus and an active service/maintenance yard, owned by Prologis with Caltrain holding a perpetual easement to operate rail. A Development Agreement is the expected approval path (precedent: Pier 70, Mission Rock, Potrero Power Station, all DAs). Adjoins Mission Bay North. OCII's December 2019 Mission Bay Land Use Map, as seen in the map image (URL added to source_doc_urls), labels N5A, N6 and N7 in this area with no land-use color and no drawn boundary, unlike the numbered Mission Bay North blocks beside it. That does not settle whether the site lies outside Mission Bay North: in the repo's copy of DataSF's redevelopment project areas layer about 41% of this polygon lies inside 'Mission Bay - North', and parcels 8701003 and 8701004 are zoned MB-O. properties.notes: The outline is the union of Assessor lots 8701004, 8701003, 3797004 and 8700001 (see the accuracy note). SF Planning Case No. 2023-000384CWP, 'SF Railyards Planning Program'. The 20-acre site at the nexus of SoMa, Mission Bay and Showplace Square: Caltrain's northern terminus and an active service/maintenance yard, owned by Prologis with Caltrain holding a perpetual easement to operate rail. A Development Agreement is the expected approval path (precedent: Pier 70, Mission Rock, Potrero Power Station, all DAs). Adjoins Mission Bay North. OCII's December 2019 Mission Bay Land Use Map, as seen in the map image (linked in this record's sources), labels N5A, N6 and N7 in this area with no land-use color and no drawn boundary, unlike the numbered Mission Bay North blocks beside it. That does not settle whether the site lies outside Mission Bay North: in DataSF's redevelopment project areas layer about 41% of this polygon lies inside 'Mission Bay - North', and parcels 8701003 and 8701004 are zoned MB-O. The map PDF and the project-area boundary have not yet been checked to settle this.

properties.accuracy_caveat: REAL, DERIVED BOUNDARY -- the outer edge is a real DataSF Assessor Parcel boundary (blklot 8722025); the two notches cut into its NW and SW corners are real OpenStreetMap building traces (the Uber towers), not estimates. The resulting shape has not been independently verified against a surveyed Chase Center site plan -- it is real-minus-real, not a single authoritative source. Two small structures inside this polygon (an oval building in the west plaza, and possibly others) remain unidentified. The shape is deliberately not trimmed to DataSF's official street centerlines: that layer shows several stale/closed street segments cutting straight through the arena bowl itself (visible as a literal cross running under the roof when the shape is drawn against the street lines) -- leftover records from the four separate plan blocks (29/30/31/32) that were consolidated into one superblock when Chase Center was built, not real current streets. Trimming against them would remove 16% of this polygon's real area, so it is left untrimmed for this stated reason, as is Pier 70's 20th Street Plaza.
properties.notes: OCII/Warriors Mission Bay South Blocks 29-32. 1 Warriors Way; DataSF's parcel data lists 7-99 Warriors Way for this parcel. Anchors an 11-acre mixed-use development (Chase Center's own description of Thrive City; Wikipedia gives a 12-acre site) including 100,000 sq ft of retail space (Wikipedia's figure for the Chase Center complex; it does not say how much of that is Thrive City) and a 35,000 sq ft public plaza. Designed by MANICA Architecture (interiors by Gensler); privately financed (Chase Center's Thrive City page: 'privately-financed complex'; Wikipedia: 'The arena was financed privately'), with a reported cost of about $1.4B (Construction Dive, Aug 6, 2019: 'the $1.4 billion Chase Center'; Wikipedia's infobox gives the same figure, marked citation needed, and its text gives an uncited $1 billion). No source read says who financed it. Opened Sept 6, 2019.

ArchDaily's 'Uber Headquarters / SHoP Architects' page credits SHoP but lists 423,000 ft2 and 2022, so it may not cover exactly these two towers; Office Snapshots credits the interiors of Buildings 3 and 4 to Huntsman Architectural Group. Both are now cited. 2026-10-12 audit corrections to the description above (text only; no change to the shape, status, use or geometry_type): (1) 'designed by SHoP Architects' is not supported for these two towers. The ArchDaily page (Year: 2022) says 'The 423,000-square-foot project includes an eleven-story tower at 1455 Third Street and a six-story structure at 1515 Third Street', and SF Standard (May 18, 2023) lists 1455 and 1515 Third St as two other buildings of Uber's four-building campus beside 1725 and 1655. properties.digitized_from: Assessor lot: both hulls lie inside lot 9900068 (98% of the outline). DataSF's 'Parcels - Active and Retired' dataset (acdm-wktn), queried by lot number on 2026-10-10 and read again on 2026-10-11, lists Assessor lot 9900068 in block 9900 (lot 068), marked active, with a recorded drop date of 2018-10-02. The dataset's own description of its recorded-drop-date column reads 'This is the date that the documents related the to dropping/retiring of the parcel was recorded, as tracked by Public Works.' The same row has no map-drop date, is flagged active, and is on the Assessor's secured roll in the copy dated 2026-10-01. The dataset does not say why a recorded drop date and an active flag appear together, so this record states only what the row shows. The lot is the whole shipyard lot, not an outline of the two hulls: the traced hulls cover 18% of it. Port structures carry no street name in that dataset, so a search for PIER-numbered street names finds nothing. Outline: two hand-traced hull outlines -- Dry Dock No. 2 and the Eureka Dry Dock -- on Esri World Imagery (zoom 20, imagery captured 2025-08-29). The earlier placeholder box lay in open water north of the shipyard. Hulls were told apart by length. The Port Commission memo (Calendar Item 9A, 2026-01-09, PDF p. 3) says: 'DD2 is a 900-foot single-section steel floating dry dock constructed by the Bethlehem Steel Corporation in 1970.' Mission Local (2026-02-23) says: 'Dry Dock No. 2, which was built in 1970, ...' and 'The adjacent dry dock, Eureka, which was built in 1945, is 528 feet long'. Potrero View (2026-07-15) gives the Eureka as longer: 'Eureka Drydock is 570 feet.' The sources disagree on the Eureka's length (528 ft is 161 m; 570 ft is 174 m) and agree on its 1945 build. The large eastern hull measures about 283 m (Dry Dock No. 2: 900 ft is 274 m) and the central hull about 169 m including wing walls, so the central hull is the shorter dock whichever Eureka length is right. No source read says which hull sits where, so this match is Pier & Point's own inference. Still no Port GIS layer or site-plan figure to trace from.

Port staff anticipate advertising a demolition-services contract in summer 2026 for Dry Dock No. 2 and the neighboring Eureka Dry Dock (a second floating dry dock at Piers 68/70, formerly USS Steadfast/AFDM-14, per Marine Log, 2025-07-24, reporting the Port's request-for-proposals notice, which calls it formerly known as Steadfast (AFDM 14) -- not the 1890 ferryboat Eureka at Hyde Street Pier/SF Maritime NHP). Total estimated cost of stabilization and disposal is $61.2M (Capital Planning Committee memo, 2026-02-09); see the record file for the funding breakdown and what remains unfunded.

Pier 38 is lot 9900038 and Pier 40 is lot 9900040 (DataSF lists both as active, block 9900, the pier number as the lot, street name KING), and the earlier traces lie 95% inside the two lots together, so the match is clear; no Port document read names the lots. Status 'planned' means proposed only: the Port's April 28, 2026 staff report says the term sheet 'was never executed' and that the Port and developer agreed to 'suspend active negotiation of transaction documents' for twelve months 'to further evaluate project costs and other key obstacles to Project feasibility'; completing environmental (CEQA) analysis and executing a lease are still future benchmarks. properties.regulatory_context: Developer: San Francisco Waterfront Partners III, LLC (SFWP), an affiliate of Pacific Waterfront Partners (PWP). Original Exclusive Negotiating Agreement: Port Commission Resolution 21-10 (2021-02-23), expired 2023-03-15 for missed performance dates. PWP separately owed the Port over $980,000 in back rent on three unrelated leases (Pier 28, two Agriculture Building suites), unpaid since it vacated them 2024-01-31. On 2026-04-28 the Port Commission adopted a Settlement Agreement (Resolution 26-21: PWP to pay $720,000 over 3 years, with the remainder of the debt forgiven on compliance) and an Amended and Restated ENA (Resolution 26-22: a 12-month 'Evaluation Period' to explore value engineering, project phasing and a new financial partner, with a new Schedule of Performance due before the period ends around April 2027). No lease, term sheet or CEQA review is in place as of this record's own last_verified date.
properties.notes: The outline is Assessor lots 9900038 (Pier 38) and 9900040 (Pier 40) (see the accuracy note). The 2022 scope estimate (~215,000 sq ft office, up to 20,000 sq ft retail, ~$528-536M cost) is explicitly under review ('value engineering', 'scope reduction') per the April 2026 Amended ENA and is not treated as current. Separately, an August 2026 marketing listing ('Pacific Cornerstone') offers up to ~279,876 sq ft of the piers for long-term lease to credit tenants, positioning occupancy for late 2029 -- parallel tenant-marketing activity alongside the Port's own Evaluation Period, not a confirmed deal.

properties.project_name: 22nd St Caltrain Station ADA Access Improvement -- adjacent to Pier 70
properties.digitized_from: The owner's direction (2026-10-13): the existing station sits under the I-280 viaduct, south of 22nd St. Placement is a coarse locational box in that spot, built from DataSF's official street centerlines: 60 m across (centred on the I-280 corridor between its two carriageway centerlines), running 80 m south from the 22nd St curb line (6.8 m from its centerline). No Caltrain/Peninsula Corridor Joint Powers Board GIS shapefile or site-plan figure was available, and the platforms are hidden from aerial imagery by the elevated freeway, so its size is a placeholder, not a measurement. DataSF's Assessor layer has no lot of its own for the station's tracks (active rail right-of-way); about half of the box lies in active lot 4168011 (zoned Public), which no source read names as the station's lot.

properties.accuracy_caveat: APPROXIMATE -- a coarse placeholder box (60 m by 80 m) under the I-280 viaduct just south of 22nd St, where the owner places the existing below-grade station; not a traced footprint of the platforms or the planned ramps themselves (one ~305ft ramp on the northbound platform, one ~465ft ramp on the southbound platform, per the project's own design description). The platforms are hidden from aerial imagery by the freeway above, so the box's size and exact position are not measured. The box is not clipped against the I-280 street lines: the station is below grade, beneath the viaduct, so the freeway's own footprint is not a reason to cut it.
properties.why_no_real_parcel: The station's tracks and platforms are active Caltrain rail right-of-way with no lot of their own in the Assessor layer, the same situation as the existing 4th & King Street Station (mapped in Pier & Point's Mission Bay railyards record). About 51% of this placeholder box lies in active lot 4168011 (zoned Public, on the secured roll), a much larger lot of which the box covers 19%; no source read names that lot as the station, so it is not used as the outline.
properties.regulatory_context: The Caltrain 22nd Street Station is the railroad's only regular-service station that is not wheelchair accessible: its platforms sit about 25 ft below street level, reachable only by stairs. Sponsor: Peninsula Corridor Joint Powers Board (Caltrain); funded in part through SFCTA's Prop L. Total project cost per SFCTA's April 2026 Board Packet: $19,134,000 (Planning/Conceptual Engineering $734,000 already spent via Prop K; Design Engineering $1,300,000 via Prop L, approved by the SFCTA Board 2026-04-14 and given final approval 2026-04-28; Construction $17,100,000, an engineer's estimate at 30% design). The FTA's 'All Stations Accessibility Program' separately awarded the Peninsula Corridor Joint Powers Board $14.1 million for this project's ADA improvements, announced in September 2026 (the day is not given by the sources read) -- matching almost exactly the funding gap SFCTA's own April 2026 plan had left as 'Planned TBD'.
properties.notes: Design (PS&E) is scheduled to run April/June 2026 through July/September 2027 (30% complete as of March 2026); construction is not slated to start until spring 2028, with project completion (last eligible expenditure) targeted July/September 2029 and opening for use April/June 2029 in the same form; the same packet's project description says December 2029 (subject to funding).
